pages.title: What this unit is about
pages.body:
> 📝 **Strand 2 — Productivity Software**
Sub-strand 4: Introduction to Electronic Spreadsheet

Built-in functions turn Excel into a powerful calculator. In this unit you will use common functions, write complex formulas for percentages, commission and interest, copy formulas correctly with relative and absolute references, and fix formula errors.

pages.title: Formulas and Built-in Functions
pages.body:
Curriculum indicator B8.2.4.1.1
> 🎯 **Learning objectives** By the end of this lesson you should be able to:
- explain the difference between formulas and functions;
- access built-in functions;
- use SUM, AVERAGE, COUNT, COUNTA, COUNTIF, MAX and MIN.
A **formula** is any calculation you write, e.g. =B2+C2+D2. A **function** is a ready-made formula built into Excel with a name and **arguments** in brackets, e.g. =SUM(B2:D2). Functions are shorter, faster to write and less error-prone, especially for large ranges.
| **Function** | **Purpose** | **Example** | **Result for B2:B6 = 60, 75, 48, 90, 75** |
|---|---|---|---|
| SUM | Adds numbers | =SUM(B2:B6) | 348 |
| AVERAGE | Arithmetic mean | =AVERAGE(B2:B6) | 69.6 |
| COUNT | Counts cells containing **numbers** | =COUNT(B2:B6) | 5 |
| COUNTA | Counts **non-empty** cells (numbers or text) | =COUNTA(A1:A6) | 6 (includes the heading) |
| COUNTIF | Counts cells that meet a condition | =COUNTIF(B2:B6,">=70") | 3 |
| MAX | Largest value | =MAX(B2:B6) | 90 |
| MIN | Smallest value | =MIN(B2:B6) | 48 |
> 🪜 **Step by step — Accessing built-in functions**
1. Click the cell for the answer.
2. Use **Home › Editing › AutoSum** (Σ) and its arrow for Sum, Average, Count Numbers, Max and Min; or
3. Click **Formulas › Insert Function** (**fx**), search for a function, click **OK**, and enter the range in the **Function Arguments** box; or
4. Type the function directly: =AVERAGE( then drag over the range, type ) and press **Enter**.

pages.title: Complex Formulas
pages.body:
Curriculum indicator B8.2.4.1.2
> 🎯 **Learning objectives** By the end of this lesson you should be able to:
- create formulas for percentages, commissions and interest;
- combine functions and operators.
A **complex formula** combines several operations, cell references, functions and brackets. Remember **BODMAS**.
| **Calculation** | **Mathematics** | **Excel formula** |
|---|---|---|
| Percentage score | mark ÷ total × 100 | =B2/C2∗100 (or =B2/C2 formatted as %) |
| Percentage increase | (new − old) ÷ old × 100 | =(C2-B2)/B2∗100 |
| Sales commission at 5% | sales × 5% | =B2∗5% |
| Simple interest | I = P × R × T ÷ 100 | =B2C2D2/100 |
| Amount after interest | A = P + I | =B2+E2 |
| Discounted price (10% off) | price × (1 − 0.10) | =B2∗(1-10%) |
| Average of three tests as % of 300 | (t1 + t2 + t3) ÷ 300 × 100 | =SUM(B2:D2)/300∗100 |
> ✏️ **Worked example — Simple interest project**
|  | **A** | **B** | **C** | **D** | **E** | **F** |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Customer | Principal (GH₵) | Rate (%) | Time (yrs) | Interest | Amount |
| 2 | Esi | 2,000 | 12 | 2 | =B2C2D2/100 → 480 | =B2+E2 → 2,480 |
| 3 | Musah | 5,000 | 10 | 3 | =B3C3D3/100 → 1,500 | =B3+E3 → 6,500 |

lessons.title: Copying Formulas, Cell References and Correcting Errors

pages.title: Copying Formulas, Cell References and Correcting Errors
pages.body:
Curriculum indicator B8.2.4.1.3
> 🎯 **Learning objectives** By the end of this lesson you should be able to:
- copy and paste formulas;
- use relative and absolute references;
- correct common formula errors.
When you copy a formula, Excel adjusts the cell references automatically. This is a **relative reference**. Sometimes a reference must stay fixed, for example a single tax rate or exchange rate cell. This is an **absolute reference**, written with dollar signs: $B$2.
[[fig:c8-f11|Figure 10: Relative and absolute references when copying formulas down]]
| **Reference type** | **Example** | **When copied** |
|---|---|---|
| Relative | A2 | Both column and row change |
| Absolute | $A$2 | Nothing changes |
| Mixed | $A2 or A$2 | Only the part without $ changes |
> ✨ **Did you know?** While editing a formula, click a reference and press **F4** to cycle through A2 → $A$2 → A$2 → $A2.
> 🪜 **Step by step — Copying a formula**
1. Select the cell with the formula and press **Ctrl + C**, then select the destination cells and press **Ctrl + V**; or
2. Drag the **fill handle** down or across; or
3. Double-click the fill handle to copy the formula down to the end of the data.

pages.title: Common formula errors and how to fix them
pages.body:
## Common formula errors and how to fix them
| **Error** | **Meaning** | **Fix** |
|---|---|---|
| ##### | Column too narrow to show the number (or a negative date) | Widen the column |
| #DIV/0! | Division by zero or by an empty cell | Check the divisor; enter data |
| #NAME? | Excel does not recognise a name, e.g. misspelt function =SUMM( | Correct the spelling; put text in quotes |
| #VALUE! | Wrong type of data, e.g. adding text to a number | Check the cells contain numbers |
| #REF! | A referenced cell was deleted | Undo, or rewrite the formula |
| #N/A | A value is not available (lookup not found) | Check the lookup value |
| Circular reference | A formula refers to its own cell, e.g. =A1+B1 typed in A1 | Move the formula to another cell |
> 💻 **Practical session — Project: shop sales and commission**
Create a sheet with 8 sales agents and their monthly sales in GH₵. In one cell (e.g. F1) type the commission rate 5%. Use a formula with an **absolute reference** to calculate each agent’s commission (=B3∗$F$1), then use SUM, AVERAGE, MAX, MIN, COUNT and COUNTIF (agents with sales above GH₵10,000). Change the rate to 7% and observe every commission update. Finally, add a simple interest table as in the worked example.
